If you truly have troubles sleeping at night you should include bonds in your portfolio. It’s the only sound and empirical advice. But if you’re having a long investment horizon it’s best to just keep on DCA:ing. 

Trying to bet against the market by diversifying in to other markets is essentially stock picking. It also begs the question why you’re taking one aspect (AI-bubble) in to the equation while you’re ignoring others.

Adding small percentages of Small cap, emerging markets, and your home market are good diversifiers, but adding totally random markets like the Canadian or European are imho a bad idea.

Also Dividend Aristocrats is a good possibility and histrorically does better on downturns. Or sth like L&G Global Quality Dividend. Its a valid mix of more solid, stable non-tech what reduces impact and its less interest sensitive.

For UK investors, accumulating mmfs are subject to ERI each year. For mmfs, this means the ERI is classed as interest and thus tax at income tax rates. Am I correct? Even if you get a distribution mmf, the dividends actually count as interest and counts towards your annual tax free allowance.
No mmfs in an isa or sipp there is no interest at all.  ROYAL LONDON MMF or CSH2.
​​@BuiltByGraftsure, but the limit would be 21k tax free for basic rate tax payers in accessible ISA, any more and you are getting taxed at 24% next year on interest.

​@steve6375£20K invested in an ISA and £1K in interest earned is tax free for a basic rate taxpayer (reduced to £500 interest earned for a 40p tax payer). This is called the Personal Savings Allowance(PSA). For 45p taxpayers the PSA is £0. Premium bonds are also tax free. The coupons from UK gilts (UK government bonds) are taxable, but there is no capital gains tax on growth in value of UK gilts.
​@steve6375since when is interest taxed in an ISA? They were talking about taxing from april next year but Healey scrapped that.

Yeah, but by doing this, you are practically making a bet against the market. I believe that excluding the US is a big mistake. A more sensible approach is to keep investing in a broadly diversified global ETF such as VWCE or VALL while adding a small tilt to value stocks and/or small cap stocks, which reduced your exposure to tech and AI and is actually backed by academic evidence (namely research from Fama & French and others).

If your retired with pensions covering daily expenditure, no debt, reserve emergency fund then invest large companies medium/high risk, medium dividend yield spend high in good years, opposite in bad years, never sell at a lost. Never bonds , boring, It makes life more interesting and occupies your mind and you are always protected whatever the market does. Sleep well but get enjoyment from playing with your investments as a hobby.

lol never bonds sounds great until you get hit with a 30% drop right when tech cools off. I used to think the same way with my $1.8M portfolio, but managing individual dividend picks during pullbacks became a full-time stress job. Ended up restructuring with an independent fiduciary who set up a tax-smart floor for my withdrawal needs. Now I still trade a small bucket for fun, but the main wealth is completely insulated without relying on bonds.

Honestly going through this exact dilemma right now with my tech gains... who did you end up using to set up that floor structure?? my CPA is useless when it comes to actual allocation strategy and I really need a second opinion.

My long term way of global investing is clear. 2 ETFs, the first one is for beeing invested in the overall global economy, the second one is here for bringing down the technology sector exposure just a little bit and raise other sectors like consumer staples, energy, health care, etc... in the same move. My choice is:

~ 70% Vanguard FTSE All-World
~ 30% Vanguard FTSE All-World High Dividend Yield

Mine are both accumulating, but that's clearly personal preference.

I wouldn't bet on a high dividends ETF if I were you. While a lot of investors like the illusion of dividends, it is not backed by evidence. A more sensible approach is maybe tilting the portfolio to value stocks and/or small cap stocks which is clearly supported by academic evidence (namely by research from Fama & French). In addition, having some bonds is also crucial for achieving an asset allocation that is inline with your own risk tolerance. That's again supported by evidence, namely by Nobel Laureate Harry Markowitz with his Modern Portfolio Theory.

​@wiseinvestormeHi! I'm not a fan of the dividend strategy either. The dividend ETF I chose doesn't pay out direct dividends since it's accumulating. Instead, it aims solely at weighting sectors more evenly.
​As for bonds: despite my very long investment horizon, I've parked some cash in a money market fund. This could cover my living expenses for a few months if I ever need to access my savings while global stock markets happen to be in the red.
Best regards
